definition: The ancient Greek term for acting against your own better judgment - knowing the right thing to do and doing something else anyway.
The distance between what you decide to do and what you actually do; across the research, intentions explain only about 28% of behavior.
People who fully intend to act but never do - the group where almost the entire knowing-doing gap actually lives.
The repeating cycle behind every habit - cue, craving, response, reward - which you reprogram one stage at a time rather than by trying harder.
What happens if you do nothing; the single strongest nudge there is, because doing nothing is always the easiest available action.
Any small cost or extra step between you and an action; adding or removing even 20 seconds of it changes behavior more than new knowledge does.
The built-in habit of treating right now as far more valuable than any later moment, so anything in the future instantly loses roughly a third of its worth.
Judging a decision solely by its single outcome, which teaches the wrong lessons in anything that has luck mixed into the result.
A goal defined by actions fully under your control ("train four times a week") rather than an outcome the world decides - far more effective and less demoralizing.
The now-disputed idea that willpower drains like a fuel tank during the day; large replication studies found the effect close to zero.
Focused practice at the edge of your ability with clear goals and immediate feedback - what actually builds skill, unlike simply logging comfortable hours.
Creating an obstacle in advance so a possible failure has a ready excuse - a self-protection strategy that shields self-worth at the cost of results.
The skill of judging what to build and why it matters to a real person - choosing the right thing to make, not just making things well.
The ability to see and feel a product from the user's point of view - their goal, their confusion, their fear - instead of your own expert perspective.
The idea that people "hire" a product to make progress in their lives; nobody wants a drill, they want the hole - so design for the goal, not the feature.
The picture in a user's head of how something works; software feels obvious when it matches that picture and confusing when it fights it.
What an object lets you do - a button affords pressing, a slider affords dragging. It is the action the thing makes possible.
The visible cue that tells you an affordance exists - the underline that says "link," the raised edge that says "press me." Without it, a feature is effectively hidden.
The gap between what a user wants to do and figuring out how to do it in the interface - "I want to refund this order, but where is that button?"
The gap between the system doing something and the user understanding that it happened - "did my changes actually save, or did I just lose an hour of work?"
The total mental effort a screen demands; the more a user must hold in their head at once, the heavier and more tiring the product feels.
The more choices you show, the longer a decision takes; the practical fix is to trim options or reveal them in stages so users decide faster.
People can hold only about seven items (give or take two) in short-term memory at once, so information should be grouped and chunked to fit.
The bigger and closer a target, the faster it is to hit; make important buttons large and reachable, and dangerous ones small and far.
Users spend most of their time on other products, so they expect yours to work the same way; inventing a brand-new pattern mostly invents new confusion.
It is far easier to recognize an option that is shown than to recall one from memory, which is why menus beat blank command lines for most people.
Showing only what is needed now and revealing advanced options later, so beginners are not overwhelmed and experts are not blocked.
Deliberate limits that prevent errors by making the wrong action impossible - like greying out "Submit" until a form is valid.
How easily a user can find a feature or figure out what is possible without being told; high discoverability means the product teaches itself.
Shaping how a product feels - trust, calm, delight - not just whether it functions; two apps can do the same task while one feels like a friend and the other like a tax form.
People judge an experience mostly by its most intense moment and its ending, not its average - so design strong peaks and clean endings.
A design that tricks or pressures users into acting against their own interest - the hidden unsubscribe link, the sneaky pre-checked box - working short-term and corroding trust long-term.
Once you know how something works you cannot imagine not knowing, which makes experts blind to what confuses beginners - and the worst judges of their own designs.
Walking through an interface against a short checklist of usability rules of thumb (classically Jakob Nielsen's ten) to catch obvious problems without a formal study.
A user-interview method: ask about real past behavior, never about your idea, with questions so grounded in facts that even your mom couldn't accidentally mislead you.
Breaking a problem down to its most fundamental, verifiable truths and building conclusions up from those alone, ignoring how it has always been done.
Solving a problem by copying what already exists; efficient and good for incremental improvement, but it can never escape the assumptions baked into the template.
A root-cause technique from Toyota: ask "Why?" five times in a row, each time targeting the previous answer, to move from a surface symptom to the real cause.
A four-step learning loop: pick a concept, explain it in plain language as if to a child, find where the explanation breaks down, then simplify and repeat.
Seeing a problem as a web of stocks, flows, delays, and feedback loops rather than isolated parts, so you can predict how it will push back over time.
A feedback loop that amplifies whatever is already happening, producing exponential growth or runaway collapse - the compound interest of systems.
A feedback loop that resists change and pushes a system back toward a target, like a thermostat clicking the heat on and off.
A place in a system where a small change produces a large, lasting effect; the strongest of all is the paradigm - the shared beliefs the system was built on.
The tendency of a system to neutralize your fix - add highway lanes to cut traffic and you often induce more driving, recreating the jam.
Asking "and then what?" beyond the first result of a decision, tracing the chain of later consequences - the antidote to choices that feel good now but cause damage later.
Working backward from the failure you most want to avoid; as the mathematician Carl Jacobi put it, "invert, always invert."
Imagining your plan has already failed and working back to what caused it, which surfaces risks that optimism normally hides.
The domain where your understanding is genuinely reliable; knowing where its edge lies matters as much as knowing what is inside it.
Charlie Munger's idea of wiring together frameworks from many fields so several lenses hit one decision at once, instead of forcing everything through a single tool.
The value of the best alternative you give up; every "yes" is a "no" to everything else you could have done with the same time or money.
The historical average for similar cases - what Kahneman calls the "outside view" - a powerful antidote to overconfidence in your own specific situation.
Fast, automatic, effortless thinking that handles most daily decisions using shortcuts; efficient but predictably error-prone.
Slow, deliberate, effortful analysis that can override System 1's errors but tires quickly - which is why good defaults matter so much.
A mental shortcut that makes judgment fast and usually good enough, but fails in predictable, named ways when the situation doesn't fit the rule of thumb.
Noticing and remembering only the evidence that fits what you already believe, while quietly discounting everything that disagrees.
Leaning too hard on the first number you see when estimating something; you adjust away from it but almost never far enough.
When the wording of a choice changes which option you pick even though the facts are identical - "90% fat-free" and "10% fat" describe the same food.
Judging how likely something is by how easily an example comes to mind, so vivid or recent events feel common even when they are rare.
The pull to keep things as they are because change takes effort and doing nothing feels safer, which is what makes default options so powerful.
Valuing something more simply because you own it, so you demand more to give it up than you would have paid to get it.
Losses hurt about twice as much as equivalent gains feel good, so people work harder to avoid losing than to win the same amount.
Throwing good resources after a failing path because of what you already spent; spent is spent, and it should never drive the next decision.
Systematically overrating the accuracy of your own judgment, which makes forecasts too narrow and blinds you to how often you are wrong.
Kahneman and Tversky's account of how people actually weigh gains, losses, and risk - from a reference point, with losses looming larger than gains.
The urge to give back when someone gives to us first; it works even with tiny, unwanted gifts, which is why free samples reliably lift spending.
Looking to what others are doing to decide what is correct, especially under uncertainty - the engine behind reviews, wait-lists, and "bestseller" tags.
Wanting something more as it becomes rarer or more urgent; "only 2 left" and "ends tonight" work by making a loss feel imminent.
Deferring to perceived experts or symbols of authority - titles, uniforms, credentials - even when the claim itself deserves scrutiny.
A brain messenger that fires for surprise and anticipation rather than pleasure, driving wanting rather than liking - the pull behind cravings and habits.
Generating many varied ideas without judging them, where quantity and variety are the goal; converge too early and you kill creativity.
Narrowing a pile of options down to the best one; the necessary partner to divergent thinking, but destructive if used too soon.
The creative stage where you deliberately step away from a problem so your unconscious keeps making associations and hands you the "shower idea."
Carol Dweck's finding that abilities like creativity can be developed with effort; it consistently produces more output and resilience than a fixed mindset.
The belief that talent is innate and unchangeable, which quietly discourages effort and makes people quit the moment something feels hard.
B = MAP: a behavior happens only when Motivation, Ability, and a Prompt converge; raising ability by cutting friction is the most reliable lever.
An "I will [behavior] at [time] in [place]" plan; Peter Gollwitzer's research shows this simple format doubles or triples follow-through.
Anchoring a new habit to an existing one - "After I [current habit], I will [new habit]" - borrowing the neural pathway that is already firing reliably.
Shrinking any new habit to a two-minute version, because starting is the hard part and a started habit is far easier to continue than to begin.
Tying a habit to who you are ("I am a runner") so each repetition becomes a vote for that identity rather than a chore to endure.
The rule that one missed day is an accident but two in a row is the start of a new bad habit, so you always show up the next day.
A single habit that drags other good behaviors along with it; exercise is the classic, quietly improving sleep, diet, and focus without you targeting them.
The frustrating stretch where effort accumulates invisibly before results break through - like ice doing nothing at 25°F, then melting at 32°F.
The gap between an expected and an actual reward; dopamine fires most when a cue is recognized in anticipation, not just when the reward finally lands.
A payoff that varies unpredictably, producing the compulsive pull behind slot machines, social feeds, and notification badges.
